plans.objective: [DIM: structure] The rigid family is defined by a set of linear algebraic constraints that reduce the solution space to a finite-dimensional affine subspace, where the minimum network width $N_c(w)$ is bounded by the dimension of the basis functions (e.g., polynomials or trigonometric functions) required to represent the solution; the fat family consists of high-degree random polynomials with a solution space dimension that grows combinatorially with the number of constraints, making $N_c(w)$ unbounded within $h \leq 64$. | This hypothesis is the most testable and novel because it provides a clear mathematical framework for distinguishing between rigid and fat families based on algebraic structure, which can be directly verified through numerical experiments. It also aligns with the known results in polynomial interpolation and approximation theory, making it a strong candidate for further investigation. |

steps.description: Implement the rigid and fat family functions as described in the hypothesis, ensuring proper normalization of y/yv to O(1) and maintaining (N,1) shape for all arrays. The rigid family will be a low-dimensional polynomial/trigonometric set that can be uniquely determined by w points, while the fat family will be high-degree random polynomials that cannot be uniquely determined within h≤64. We'll create the family function that returns training and validation constraints for both families.

plans.objective: [DIM: measure] The heldout error for the rigid family follows a U-shaped curve as a function of sample width w: it initially decreases as w increases from underfitting regimes, but eventually increases due to over-constrained sampling causing numerical ill-conditioning in the constraint matrix.

steps.description: [auto-routed: surprise=1.00] Implement the family function for rigid and fat families with proper O(1) normalization and (N,1) shaped outputs, ensuring held-out points are non-overlapping. First verify rigid family anchor point (h=2~8, max abs error ≤1e-3) before scanning widths. Use two-layer tanh networks with L-BFGS-B optimization as specified in capacity_scan.

plans.objective: [DIM: structure] The rigid family is defined by a set of linear algebraic constraints that reduce the solution space to a finite-dimensional subspace spanned by orthogonal polynomials, enabling exact interpolation with width-independent capacity. | This hypothesis is most testable: it directly predicts N_c(w) = O(1) for rigid families (flat/decreasing trend) and N_c(w) = ∞ for fat families (unreachable), matching the binary判别 criterion. It also aligns with the "scale discipline" requirement (polynomials can be normalized to O(1)) and avoids analogies to materials/chemistry. To falsify: if N_c(w) grows super-linearly with w for the rigid family, the hypothesis fails. To test: implement family(kind='rigid', w, seed) using orthogonal polynomials (e.g., Legendre) with w linear constraints, then run capacity_scan(h=[2,4,8,16,32,64], seeds=3) to verify N_c ≤ 8 and flat trend.

steps.description: [auto-routed: surprise=1.00] Implement `family(kind='rigid', w, seed)` using orthogonal polynomials (Legendre) with w linear constraints, ensuring y/yv are normalized to O(1) and Xv/X are disjoint. Include capacity_scan(h=[2,4,8,16,32,64], seeds=3) to measure N_c(w) and verify flat/decreasing trend.

plans.objective: [DIM: measure] The heldout error of the rigid family follows a sub-Gaussian tail bound $P(\text{err} > \epsilon) \leq C \exp(-w^2 \epsilon^2 / \sigma^2)$ due to the low VC-dimension of the constrained solution space, whereas the fat family exhibits heavy-tailed error distributions (Pareto $\alpha \approx 1.5$) from high-variance coefficient landscapes.
